title: Binomial distribution
summary: A [[binomial-distribution|binomial distribution]] counts the successes in a fixed number of [[independent-events|independent]] [[trial|trials]], each with the same chance of success. You write $X \sim \mathrm{B}(n, p)$, find its probabilities on your GDC, and use $\mathrm{E}(X) = np$ for the number of successes to expect.

goals.text: Decide whether a situation fits a [[binomial-distribution|binomial distribution]], and write it as $X \sim \mathrm{B}(n, p)$.
Find $\mathrm{P}(X = r)$ by hand for small cases and with your GDC for the rest.
Turn "at most", "at least", "fewer than", "more than" and "between" into the right GDC calculation.
Find the mean, [[variance|variance]] and [[standard-deviation|standard deviation]] of $X \sim \mathrm{B}(n, p)$, and work back from them to $n$ and $p$.
Use $np$ as the expected number of successes, the same idea as the expected number of occurrences.

synonyms: mean and variance of a binomial
number of successes in n trials

before.hint: ${}^{n}C_{r} = \frac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}$. Or count the ways to choose $2$ things from $6$.

before.prompt: A [[random-variable|random variable]] $Y$ takes the values $0$, $1$ and $2$ with probabilities $0.5$, $0.3$ and $0.2$. Find $\mathrm{E}(Y)$.
before.hint: Multiply each value by its probability, then add.

blocks.text: Plant $10$ seeds. Each one grows with probability $0.6$, whatever the others do. The number that grow could be anything from $0$ to $10$. A binomial distribution gives the probability of each.
Each seed is a [[trial|trial]] with two results. The result you count is a success (it grows); the other is a failure. "Success" is only a label: it could be a faulty part.

blocks.statement: Let $X$ be the number of successes in $n$ trials. $X$ has a [[binomial-distribution|binomial distribution]], written $X \sim \mathrm{B}(n, p)$, when all four conditions hold: the number of trials $n$ is fixed; each trial has two outcomes, success or failure; the probability of success $p$ is the same in every trial; the trials are [[independent-events|independent]].
blocks.plain: You repeat the same yes-or-no experiment a set number of times and count the yeses.

blocks.text: Independent means the result of one trial doesn't change the chances for any other. You met independent events in {{lesson:4.6}}. Read $X \sim \mathrm{B}(n, p)$ as "$X$ is binomial with $n$ trials and success probability $p$".

blocks.question: A fair six-sided die is rolled $20$ times. $X$ is the number of rolls that show a $1$ or a $2$. Explain why $X$ can be modelled by a binomial distribution, and state the values of $n$ and $p$.
steps: Each roll is a success (a $1$ or a $2$) or a failure, and the number of rolls is fixed: $n = 20$.
The die is fair, so every roll succeeds with the same probability, $p = \frac{2}{6} = \frac{1}{3}$.
One roll does not affect another, so the rolls are independent. All four conditions hold: $X \sim \mathrm{B}\left(20, \frac{1}{3}\right)$.

blocks.question: A bag holds $7$ green and $3$ yellow counters. Four counters are taken out one at a time, and $X$ is the number of green ones. Is $X$ binomial when (a) each counter is put back before the next is taken; (b) the counters are not put back? If it is, state $n$ and $p$.
steps: (a) Every draw is from the same $10$ counters, so $\mathrm{P}(\text{green}) = \frac{7}{10} = 0.7$ each time. The $4$ draws are independent, so $X \sim \mathrm{B}(4, 0.7)$.
(b) The first counter is green with probability $\frac{7}{10}$. If it was green, $6$ of the $9$ counters left are green. So the second is green with probability $\frac{6}{9}$.
The probability of success changes from draw to draw. So in (b), $X$ is not binomial.

blocks.text: Using a binomial model when items are taken [[without-replacement|without replacement]]. Before you write $\mathrm{B}(n, p)$, check that $p$ is the same on every trial.

blocks.prompt: A card is drawn from a standard pack of $52$ cards, noted and put back. This is done $10$ times. $X$ is the number of hearts drawn, and $X \sim \mathrm{B}(10, p)$. Find $p$.
blocks.hint: A standard pack has $13$ hearts. Does putting the card back change anything?
blocks.explain: $13$ of the $52$ cards are hearts, so $p = \frac{13}{52} = \frac{1}{4}$ on every draw. Putting the card back keeps $p$ the same, so the model holds.

blocks.prompt: Eight sweets are taken one at a time, without replacement, from a jar of $12$ lemon and $18$ orange sweets. $X$ is the number of lemon sweets taken. Which binomial condition fails?
blocks.hint: Work out the chance that the second sweet is lemon, given that the first one was.

options.text: The probability of success changes from one draw to the next
The number of trials is not fixed
Each trial has more than two outcomes

blocks.explain: The first sweet is lemon with probability $\frac{12}{30}$. If it was, the second is lemon with probability $\frac{11}{29}$, so $p$ is not constant. There are still $8$ trials, and each is lemon or not lemon.

sections.heading: The probability of exactly r successes

blocks.text: Before you use a GDC, see where binomial probabilities come from. Build one small case by hand.

blocks.question: A spinner lands on red with probability $0.3$. It is spun $4$ times. Find the probability that it lands on red exactly twice.
steps: Let $X$ be the number of reds, so $X \sim \mathrm{B}(4, 0.3)$. Write R for red and N for not red, with $\mathrm{P}(\text{N}) = 1 - 0.3 = 0.7$.
One way to get two reds is RRNN. The spins are [[independent-events|independent]], so multiply: $0.3 \times 0.3 \times 0.7 \times 0.7 = 0.3^{2} \times 0.7^{2} = 0.0441$.
Other orders work too: RRNN, RNRN, RNNR, NRRN, NRNR and NNRR. That is $6$ orders, and each has probability $0.0441$.
The number of orders is the number of ways to choose which $2$ of the $4$ spins are red: ${}^{4}C_{2} = 6$.
Add the $6$ equal probabilities: $\mathrm{P}(X = 2) = 6 \times 0.0441 = 0.2646$.

blocks.text: The same reasoning works for any $n$ and $r$. Each order with $r$ successes and $n - r$ failures has probability $p^{r}(1-p)^{n-r}$. There are ${}^{n}C_{r}$ such orders: the [[binomial-coefficient|binomial coefficient]] from {{lesson:1.9}}.

This formula is not in the formula booklet. Most binomial probabilities are found on a GDC, but the formula is quick for small cases. Two special cases: $\mathrm{P}(X = 0) = (1-p)^{n}$ and $\mathrm{P}(X = n) = p^{n}$.

blocks.question: Seeds of a certain plant grow with probability $0.85$, independently of each other. Rosa plants $18$ seeds. Use your calculator to find the probability that exactly $15$ of them grow. Give your answer to 3 s.f.
steps: Let $X$ be the number of seeds that grow. There are $18$ independent trials with $p = 0.85$, so $X \sim \mathrm{B}(18, 0.85)$.
Write down what you need: $\mathrm{P}(X = 15)$.
Use binomial pdf with $n = 18$, $p = 0.85$ and $x = 15$. The GDC gives $0.240573\ldots$
Check with the formula: ${}^{18}C_{15} \times 0.85^{15} \times 0.15^{3} = 816 \times 0.087354\ldots \times 0.003375$, which is about $0.24$.
Round only at the end: $0.241$ to 3 s.f.

blocks.explain: ${}^{4}C_{3} \times \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{3} \times \frac{3}{4} = 4 \times \frac{1}{64} \times \frac{3}{4} = \frac{3}{64}$. Leaving out the $4$ gives $\frac{3}{256}$. Swapping $p$ and $1 - p$ gives $\frac{27}{64}$.

blocks.prompt: In a town, $22\%$ of households own a dog. A random sample of $16$ households is chosen. Find the probability that exactly $4$ of them own a dog. Give your answer to 3 s.f.
blocks.hint: Let $X$ be the number of dog owners, $X \sim \mathrm{B}(16, 0.22)$. Use binomial pdf with $x = 4$.

sections.heading: At most, at least and between

blocks.text: Most questions ask about a range of values, such as "at most $3$" or "at least $6$". Your GDC's binomial cdf adds $\mathrm{P}(X = 0)$ up to $\mathrm{P}(X = k)$ for you. So it gives $\mathrm{P}(X \le k)$ in one step.

Everything else comes from $\mathrm{P}(X \le k)$ and the [[complementary-events|complement]] rule. $X$ only takes whole numbers, so "fewer than $4$" means $X \le 3$, and "more than $4$" means $X \ge 5$.

blocks.tex: \begin{array}{ll} \text{at most } k & \mathrm{P}(X \le k) \\ \text{fewer than } k & \mathrm{P}(X \le k - 1) \\ \text{at least } k & \mathrm{P}(X \ge k) = 1 - \mathrm{P}(X \le k - 1) \\ \text{more than } k & \mathrm{P}(X > k) = 1 - \mathrm{P}(X \le k) \\ a \text{ to } b \text{ inclusive} & \mathrm{P}(a \le X \le b) = \mathrm{P}(X \le b) - \mathrm{P}(X \le a - 1) \end{array}

blocks.question: On any school day, the probability that Ella's bus is late is $0.2$, [[independent-events|independently]] of other days. Find the probability that the bus is late at least once in $3$ days.
steps: Let $X$ be the number of late days, so $X \sim \mathrm{B}(3, 0.2)$.
"At least once" is $X \ge 1$. Its complement is $X = 0$: the bus is on time on all $3$ days.

blocks.text: Move $k$ and switch the event in the chart below. Watch which bars are shaded. "At least $6$" starts at the bar for $6$, so its complement stops at $5$.

blocks.alt: Bar chart of a binomial distribution with 15 trials and success probability 0.25. Each bar is the probability of one number of successes, from 0 to 15. The bars for 6 or more successes are shaded, and their total probability is shown below the chart. Sliders change the number of trials, the success probability and k. A menu switches the shaded event between equal to k, at most k and at least k.

blocks.question: A quiz has $15$ multiple-choice questions, each with $4$ options and one correct answer. Tom guesses every answer at random. Use your calculator to find the probability that he gets at least $6$ correct. Give your answer to 3 s.f.
steps: Let $X$ be the number of correct answers. Each guess is right with probability $\frac{1}{4} = 0.25$, independently. So $X \sim \mathrm{B}(15, 0.25)$.
"At least $6$" is $X \ge 6$. Its complement is $X \le 5$, so $\mathrm{P}(X \ge 6) = 1 - \mathrm{P}(X \le 5)$.
Use binomial cdf with $n = 15$, $p = 0.25$ and $x = 5$: $\mathrm{P}(X \le 5) = 0.851631\ldots$
So $\mathrm{P}(X \ge 6) = 1 - 0.851631\ldots = 0.148368\ldots$, which is $0.148$ to 3 s.f.

blocks.text: Writing $\mathrm{P}(X \ge 6) = 1 - \mathrm{P}(X \le 6)$. That throws away $X = 6$, which you wanted to keep. Subtract $\mathrm{P}(X \le 5)$ instead.

blocks.hint: $X$ is a whole number, so $X < 4$ means $X \le 3$.

blocks.prompt: An archer hits the gold ring with probability $0.65$ on each arrow, independently. She shoots $20$ arrows. Find the probability that she hits the gold between $10$ and $15$ times inclusive. Give your answer to 3 s.f.
blocks.hint: Use the last row of the table: $\mathrm{P}(X \le 15) - \mathrm{P}(X \le 9)$. Why $9$ and not $10$?

blocks.prompt: A darts player hits the bullseye with probability $0.15$ on each throw, independently. She throws $10$ darts. Given that she hits at least one bullseye, find the probability that she hits exactly one. Give your answer to 3 s.f.
blocks.hint: Use $\mathrm{P}(A \mid B) = \frac{\mathrm{P}(A \cap B)}{\mathrm{P}(B)}$. "Exactly one" is inside "at least one", so the top is just $\mathrm{P}(X = 1)$.
blocks.explain: $X \sim \mathrm{B}(10, 0.15)$. $\mathrm{P}(X = 1) = 0.347425\ldots$ and $\mathrm{P}(X \ge 1) = 1 - 0.85^{10} = 0.803125\ldots$ Divide: $0.432591\ldots \approx 0.433$. Conditional probability is taught in {{lesson:4.6}}.

blocks.prompt: Each bulb in a string of party lights is faulty with probability $0.06$, independently of the others. Find the least number of bulbs $n$ for which the probability that at least one bulb is faulty is greater than $0.95$.
blocks.hint: "At least one" is the complement of "none", so $\mathrm{P}(X \ge 1) = 1 - 0.94^{n}$. Solve $1 - 0.94^{n} > 0.95$ with a GDC table or graph, then round $n$ up.
blocks.explain: You need $0.94^{n} < 0.05$, so $n > \frac{\ln 0.05}{\ln 0.94} = 48.41\ldots$ (dividing by $\ln 0.94$, which is negative, flips the inequality). $n$ is a whole number, so round up: $n = 49$. Check: $n = 48$ gives $0.9486\ldots$, too small, and $n = 49$ gives $0.9517\ldots$

blocks.text: Rounding $n$ to the nearest whole number in a "least $n$" question. $n$ must satisfy the inequality, so always round up, then check that $n - 1$ fails.
Never round $\mathrm{P}(X \le 5)$ before you subtract it from $1$ or divide by it. Keep the full GDC value, then give the final answer to 3 s.f.

Roll a fair die $60$ times. In {{lesson:4.5}} you expected $60 \times \frac{1}{6} = 10$ sixes. The number of sixes is $X \sim \mathrm{B}\left(60, \frac{1}{6}\right)$, and that expected number is just $np$.
$\mathrm{E}(X)$ is the mean of $X$: the average number of successes over many repeats of all $n$ trials. Like any expected number, it need not be a whole number.

The [[variance|variance]] measures how widely $X$ spreads around its mean. A binomial distribution has its own formula for it. Its square root is the [[standard-deviation|standard deviation]], $\sigma$.
Both formulas are in the formula booklet, and you don't need to prove them. As $1 - p < 1$, the variance is always smaller than the mean: a quick check.

blocks.question: $X \sim \mathrm{B}(50, 0.12)$. Find the mean and the variance of $X$.
steps: Mean: $\mathrm{E}(X) = np = 50 \times 0.12 = 6$.
Variance: $\mathrm{Var}(X) = np(1-p) = 6 \times 0.88 = 5.28$.
Check: the variance is smaller than the mean, as it must be. If you also need the standard deviation, it is $\sqrt{5.28} = 2.2978\ldots \approx 2.30$.

blocks.question: A factory finds that $4\%$ of its phone screens have a defect. A batch of $250$ screens is checked. (a) Find the expected number of screens with a defect. (b) Find the probability that more than the expected number have a defect. Give your answer to 3 s.f.
steps: Let $X$ be the number of screens with a defect. Assume each screen is faulty with probability $0.04$, [[independent-events|independently]]. Then $X \sim \mathrm{B}(250, 0.04)$.
(a) The expected number is the mean: $\mathrm{E}(X) = np = 250 \times 0.04 = 10$.
(b) "More than $10$" is $X \ge 11$, so $\mathrm{P}(X > 10) = 1 - \mathrm{P}(X \le 10)$.
Binomial cdf gives $\mathrm{P}(X \le 10) = 0.583057\ldots$, so $\mathrm{P}(X > 10) = 0.416942\ldots$, which is $0.417$ to 3 s.f.

blocks.question: $X \sim \mathrm{B}(n, p)$, with $\mathrm{E}(X) = 12$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X) = 8.4$. Find $n$ and $p$.
steps: Write both facts as equations: $np = 12$ and $np(1-p) = 8.4$.
$np$ appears in both, so divide the second by the first: $1 - p = \frac{8.4}{12} = 0.7$.
Check: $40 \times 0.3 = 12$ and $12 \times 0.7 = 8.4$. Also $n$ is a whole number, as a number of trials must be.

blocks.text: Giving $np$ as the variance, or giving the variance when the question asks for the standard deviation. $\mathrm{Var}(X) = np(1-p)$, and $\sigma$ is its square root.
At HL you also find the mean and variance of $aX + b$, for example $\mathrm{Var}(3X + 5) = 9\,\mathrm{Var}(X)$.

blocks.explain: $80 \times 0.25 \times 0.75 = 15$. $20$ is the mean, $60$ is $n(1-p)$, and $\sqrt{15}$ is the standard deviation.

blocks.prompt: The number of sixes in $n$ rolls of a fair die is $X \sim \mathrm{B}\left(n, \frac{1}{6}\right)$. The expected number of sixes is $14$. Find $n$.
blocks.hint: The expected number is $np$. Set it equal to $14$.

blocks.text: $X \sim \mathrm{B}(n, p)$ counts successes in a fixed number $n$ of independent trials, each with two outcomes and the same success probability $p$.
On your GDC, binomial pdf gives $\mathrm{P}(X = r)$ and binomial cdf gives $\mathrm{P}(X \le k)$.
$\mathrm{P}(X \ge k) = 1 - \mathrm{P}(X \le k - 1)$ and $\mathrm{P}(X > k) = 1 - \mathrm{P}(X \le k)$.
$np$ is the expected number of successes. The standard deviation is $\sqrt{np(1-p)}$.

mistakes: Writing $\mathrm{P}(X \ge k) = 1 - \mathrm{P}(X \le k)$. That removes $X = k$ as well. Use $1 - \mathrm{P}(X \le k - 1)$.
Reading "more than $6$" as $X \ge 6$. For a whole-number $X$, $X > 6$ means $X \ge 7$.
Leaving out ${}^{n}C_{r}$ in a binomial probability by hand. Without it you have found the probability of one order only.
Using the binomial for "the first success is on trial $k$". That is one fixed order, $k - 1$ failures then a success, so its probability is $(1-p)^{k-1}p$.
Swapping $p$ and $1 - p$. Decide what a success is and write down its probability $p$ first.
Rounding a GDC value, such as $\mathrm{P}(X \le 10)$, before using it again. Carry the full value and round only the final answer.
examTips: Find a binomial probability: write the distribution, $X \sim \mathrm{B}(n, p)$, and the probability statement, such as $\mathrm{P}(X \ge 6) = 1 - \mathrm{P}(X \le 5)$, before the GDC value.
Paper 1 has no GDC, so binomial work there uses the formulas: $np$, $np(1-p)$, or a small case such as $\mathrm{P}(X = 0) = (1-p)^{n}$.
Give probabilities to 3 s.f. unless the question says otherwise, and never round a value you will use again.
Find the expected number: write $np$ with the numbers in, then the value. Don't round it to a whole number.
